rationale: A wins because it has discipline: three angles, three beats, three proof paths. Its price angle is especially clean because it says the quiet part out loud: "do not claim savings pay for it." B has good instincts, but keeping "In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" as its own angle is exactly the padding A correctly refused: a metric is not automatically a story.
gaps_in_A: The trend angle overstates the category context with "Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory" and "100 stores is the pilot-to-deployment threshold this beat watches for"; those may be true, but they are not in the supplied facts.

The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is a little early for the labor and pricing angles. A founder still needs staffing-hours data, price-pledge terms, or an on-record link/no-link between automation and pricing before pitching hard.
A misses the sharper scale-skepticism buried in the facts: 100 restaurants out of 3,500+ is under 3%, which could weaken the "leave the pilot phase" framing.
gaps_in_B: B pads the robotics story into too many envelopes: "guac robot reaches 100," "automating both ends of the kitchen," and "one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" are not three fully separate stories.

"call it a pilot, not a rollout" is a punchy line, but it argues past the fact block, which says Chipotle is rolling Autocado out to 100 restaurants. Skepticism is useful; pretending the supplied rollout is not a rollout is cute and risky.

"Autocado plus the in-testing Digital Makeline reads as a coordinated strategy" overclaims. The update says Digital Makeline is being tested; it does not prove a coordinated kitchen-automation strategy.
"making the two-system pattern visible for the first time" invents timing. The facts say the systems exist in this update, not that this is the first disclosure.
